opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest starting point is that we don't know how hard this problem is. There's a world where alignment turns out to be fairly tractable, where the techniques we have now, plus some incremental progress, are enough to get systems that reliably do what we want. And there's a world where it's genuinely very hard, where capabilities outpace our ability to understand and control these systems, and the default trajectory goes badly. We don't have strong evidence that pins us to one or the other.

Given that uncertainty, I'd argue for a portfolio approach rather than betting everything on one theory of how things play out.

First, we should do the work that pays off across many scenarios. Better evaluations, better ways of measuring whether a model has dangerous capabilities or is behaving deceptively, are valuable whether alignment is easy or hard. If it's easy, good evals confirm that and let us deploy with confidence. If it's hard, they're our early warning system. Robustness research falls in the same bucket. A lot of my own work has been on adversarial robustness, and one sobering lesson is that even superhuman systems, like Go-playing AIs, can have surprisingly exploitable failure modes. That tells you capability doesn't automatically bring reliability, and that's worth knowing regardless of your priors.

Second, it's worth investing in research directions that might turn out to be dead ends, precisely because we don't know which ones will work. Interpretability, scalable oversight, formal verification, control-style approaches that assume the model might be adversarial and try to contain it anyway. Some of these will probably fail. But if you only fund the safest bets, you're implicitly assuming the problem is easy.

Third, and this matters a lot, the possibility that risks aren't fully reducible through technical work is an argument for governance and coordination. If we can't be confident we'll solve alignment in time, we want the ability to slow down, to set thresholds where developers have to demonstrate safety before scaling further, and to have institutions that can actually enforce that. Technical research and policy aren't separate tracks; good policy needs technical tools to know what to require, and technical research needs policy so that results actually change what gets deployed.

And finally, I'd say we should be trying hard to reduce the uncertainty itself. A lot of the disagreement in this field comes from people having different intuitions with very little empirical grounding. The more we can turn these questions into things we can actually test, like whether models generalize in the ways we hope, or whether deceptive behavior emerges under certain training pressures, the better our decisions get. Uncertainty isn't a reason for paralysis. It's a reason to hedge sensibly and to go find out.

r001.rationale: The response discusses evaluations, robustness research, and policy, but does not compare the cost of basic risk measures with frontier model training expenditures.

r002.rationale: It recommends better evaluations to measure dangerous capabilities and deceptive behavior, describing them as a way to confirm whether alignment is tractable or provide early warning if it is not.

r003.rationale: The response does not argue that evidence of mutual destruction at a capability threshold would reduce incentives to race toward it.

r004.rationale: It recommends a portfolio of research and mitigations across scenarios, but does not prioritize readily available measures on the grounds that they should suffice in most plausible worlds.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot. The honest answer is I don't know whether the risks are fully reducible, and I think anyone who tells you they're confident either way is overclaiming. But I don't think that uncertainty should be paralyzing, because the decision-relevant question isn't "can we drive risk to zero," it's "what actions have the best expected value across the range of worlds we might be in."

So the way I'd frame it is something like a portfolio approach. There are some worlds where alignment turns out to be basically tractable with enough engineering effort, and in those worlds the bottleneck is just that we haven't put enough serious talent and resources into things like scalable oversight, interpretability, robust evaluations. There are other worlds where the technical problem is genuinely hard, maybe not solvable on the timelines we're on, and in those worlds what matters most is governance: buying time, making sure we're not deploying systems we can't evaluate, having the institutional capacity to slow down if the warning signs show up. And then there are worlds where the risk is much lower than people like me worry about, and in those worlds the main cost of safety work is that it slowed things down a bit, which I think is a pretty acceptable downside.

What I try to do at FAR is work on the things that are robustly useful across most of those worlds. Adversarial robustness and red-teaming are a good example. If alignment is easy, you still want to know whether your safety training actually holds up under pressure, and we keep finding that it doesn't. Superhuman Go systems that lose to simple adversarial strategies, safety fine-tuning that gets undone with a few hundred examples, that kind of thing. If alignment is hard, that same evidence is exactly what policymakers and labs need to see in order to justify being more cautious. So the work pays off either way.

The other thing I'd say is that "reducible" is a bit of a false binary. Even if you can't eliminate the risk, you can usually shift the probability distribution. Getting from a situation where failures are silent and catastrophic to one where they're detectable and recoverable is enormously valuable even if the underlying system is still imperfect. A lot of safety engineering in other fields works this way. We never made aviation perfectly safe, we made it safe enough through layers of imperfect defenses, and I think that's the realistic model here too.

Where I think the uncertainty should change behavior is in how much weight we put on reversibility. If you're not sure whether a problem is solvable, you really don't want to lock in a state of the world where you've already deployed systems whose failure modes you don't understand. So I'd put a lot of emphasis on things like staged deployment, pre-deployment evaluation, and maintaining the ability to actually pull a model back if it's doing something bad. Those are cheap insurance relative to the stakes.

And then the last piece is just epistemics. We should be actively trying to resolve the uncertainty rather than treating it as a fixed background condition. A big part of why I care about empirical work is that it moves us from arguing about priors to actually having evidence. Three years ago people debated whether deceptive behavior was a real concern in language models; now we have concrete demonstrations. Each of those updates makes the overall strategy a bit less blind. So I'd say: do the robustly good things now, preserve optionality, and keep running the experiments that tell us which world we're in.

r002.rationale: It recommends evaluations and empirical experiments, but does not clearly recommend rigorous model evaluations specifically to test whether AI risks are reducible.

r003.rationale: The response does not argue that evidence of mutual destruction would reduce actors’ incentives to race toward a capability threshold.

r004.rationale: It recommends doing measures that are “robustly useful across most” plausible worlds, with adversarial robustness and red-teaming as examples.

astra-6.text:
I think we should be trying to reduce the risks while also finding out how much we can reduce them. Uncertainty here is a reason to do research, rather than a reason to assume either that everything will be fine or that the problem is hopeless.

You can make that concrete by taking a proposed safety technique and really trying to break it. Under what conditions does it work? Does it still work against an adversary who knows how the defense operates? Does it generalize beyond the situations you tested? A failure can be useful evidence, because it tells you where the next research effort needs to go.

But I’d distinguish pursuing that research from relying on its success. We should work hard to make systems safer without deploying increasingly powerful systems on the assumption that the remaining problems will get solved in time. If the evidence says our mitigations aren’t adequate, then slowing down or restricting deployment needs to remain an option.

So I’d want a portfolio: technical work to improve safety, evaluations to establish what that work actually buys us, and governance that lets us respond to the results. We don’t need to settle in advance whether risk is ultimately reducible to make progress on those things.

r002.rationale: It recommends testing proposed safety techniques under varied conditions, including against informed adversaries and beyond tested situations, to learn whether they work.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss a capability threshold destroying the actors who cross it or how that would affect incentives to race.

r004.rationale: It recommends technical safety work and evaluations, but does not prioritize readily available mitigations or say they are expected to suffice in most plausible worlds.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should treat that uncertainty as a reason to do more research, rather than as a reason to give up or assume things will work out. We don’t yet know how much of the risk we can eliminate, but we can make progress on specific problems and learn where the limits are.

There are really two things we want from that work. One is interventions that actually make systems safer. The other is better evidence about how hard the remaining problems are. If a safety technique works in a narrow setting, can we understand why it works and whether that carries over to more capable systems? If it fails, can we turn that failure into a useful test of the next approach?

At the same time, we shouldn’t make deploying increasingly powerful systems contingent on the hope that those problems will eventually be solved. We should be willing to adjust the pace based on the evidence. So I’d pursue technical risk reduction quite aggressively, while also building the ability to hold back when we can’t establish an adequate level of safety.
